papers.title: Waiting Time Prioritisation for Public and Private Providers: Evidence From Hip Replacement Surgery.
papers.abstract: Waiting times for planned health care treatments have been increasing in England and other OECD countries. One policy to reduce the impact of waiting times on patients' health is for doctors to prioritise patients according to their health status. This study tests the extent to which publicly-funded patients in poorer health are prioritised on the list, and whether prioritisation differs between public and private providers. We use hospital administrative data in 2015-2021 on hip replacements in England. Our results provide evidence of inpatient waiting-time prioritisation (from specialist addition to list to admission for surgery) based on pre-operative health with a difference of at least 15 days between patients with lowest and highest pre-operative health. The gradient becomes steeper as waiting times increase, and much steeper during COVID-19. While outpatient waiting times (from referral to specialist visit) comprise a substantial proportion of total time waited (inpatient plus outpatient), we find limited evidence of outpatient waiting time prioritisation. Differences in inpatient waiting-time prioritisation between public and private providers are mostly due to different casemix and shorter average waiting times by private providers. We also simulate the effect of prioritisation policies that reduce inpatient waiting times for patients with low pre-operative health by 20% while simultaneously increasing it for those with high pre-operative health. We find that these policies could generate health gains of 183 QALYs in a given year. We conclude that there is scope for improving prioritisation of patients on the waiting list.

papers.title: New Medical Schools, Access to Physicians, and Health Outcomes: Evidence From Japan.
papers.abstract: We analyse the impact of the construction of medical schools and associated university hospitals in Japan during the 1970s, which was primarily driven by 'One Prefecture, One Medical School Policy' (OPOMS). We find that the number of physicians increased significantly in prefectures where a medical school was built, and this effect persisted for more than 20 years. Moreover, we uncover suggestive evidence that the establishment of university hospitals may lead to a reduction in the overall mortality rate, especially among the elderly. Our results also indicate that the improvement in health outcomes is likely attributed to access to high-quality care resulting from the opening of university hospitals, rather than an overall increase in the utilisation of healthcare services.

papers.title: Smiling Muscle Stimulation Alters Neural Processing During Emotional Face Comparison.
papers.abstract: Within embodied and predictive-processing frameworks, emotional face perception is informed by bodily states, such as proprioceptive facial feedback. In line with this, our earlier work showed that activation of smiling muscles with facial neuromuscular electrical stimulation (fNMES) can induce a happiness bias in emotional face perception, and reduce visual face processing demands. Here, we extended this research to examine whether the same facial muscle stimulation biases the emotional representation of a face when it serves as a perceptual template (prime) for comparison with a following target face. In a delayed matching-to-sample task, 53 participants judged which of two sequentially presented faces appeared happier (or more female, in a control sex task). On half of trials, fNMES was applied bilaterally to the zygomaticus major during encoding of the prime face. Performance was held constant using an adaptive staircase. fNMES altered comparison judgments only when emotion was task-relevant, flattening the relation between emotion difference and choice. Across tasks, fNMES reduced N170 amplitudes and increased Early Posterior Negativity (EPN) differences between happy and sad faces. The prime EPN predicted choice only when emotion was task-relevant, whereas fNMES modulated emotion effects on the target N170 only in the control task. Facial feedback may thus increase the perceptual salience of emotion-relevant information, with task-dependent consequences for decisions.
